<<dd_version: 2>>

![](images/math-books-cartoon.png){width=45% fig-alt="Cartoon of a library: 'Who is putting the math books in the horror section?'"}

## Outcome (DV) = linear combination + error

The linear regression model:

$$y_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta x_{i} + \varepsilon_{i}$$

$${income}_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{ed\_yrs}{ed\_yrs}_{i} + \beta_{woman}{woman}_{i} + \ldots + \varepsilon_{i}$$

In matrix notation:

$$y_{i} = \mathbf{x}_{i}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \varepsilon_{i}$$

$$y_{i} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x_{i1} & \ldots & x_{ik} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \beta_{0} \\ \beta_{1} \\ \ldots \\ \beta_{k} \end{bmatrix} + \varepsilon_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{i1} + \ldots + \beta_{k}x_{ik} + \varepsilon_{i}$$

- Note the bolded $\mathbf{x}$ and the bolded $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ (beta) above is notation to denote a matrix (in this case vectors \[which is a matrix with only one row or column\])
  - This allows for compact notation to refer to many IVs ($\mathbf{x}$) and many associated coefficients ($\boldsymbol{\beta}$)
- The *x*'s have subscript *i*'s to denote they vary across each observation in the data
  - The $\beta$'s do not have subscripts because there is only one for each variable

### ε is unexplained variation

- $\varepsilon$ (epsilon) represents variation that is not explained by the IVs ($\mathbf{x}$)
  - Often called the "error term" (or "disturbance")
- No health or social science model is likely to explain anywhere close to 100% of the variation in the DV so there will be some unexplained variation
  - Unexplained variation may be due to:
    - Randomness
    - Measurement error
    - Unobserved heterogeneity
      - Some sources of error were measured but not included in your model; some sources of error are unmeasurable; etc.
- For any given observation we can calculate a prediction error---also called the **residual** for that observation (often denoted as $e_{i}$ rather than $\varepsilon_{i}$ to distinguish it from the error which is a theoretical deviation from the *true* value rather than the *observed* value)---by comparing their observed value of the DV ($y_{i}$) to what our model predicts ($\widehat{y}$) \[note a "$\widehat{hat}$" denotes a predicted value\]

$$prediction\ error = e_{i} = observed - predicted = y_{i} - {\widehat{y}}_{i}$$

## Maximum likelihood and OLS estimates of β's

- Guess the values of the coefficients: $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{*}$
  - For this guess, the residuals for case *i* are:

$$r_{i}^{*} = y_{i} - \mathbf{x}_{i}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{*} = y_{i} - {\widehat{y}}_{i}$$

- Compute the sum of squared residuals (total amount of error):

$$SSR = \sum_{i = 1}^{N}(y_{i} - \mathbf{x}_{i}\boldsymbol{\beta})^{2} = \sum_{i = 1}^{N}{r_{i}}^{2}$$

- Try other values of $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{*}$ to see if you can make *SSR* smaller
  - The ***maximum likelihood estimates*** of $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{*}$ are those that make SSR the smallest
    - Much more on this later; the general intuition is OK for now
- *The ordinary least squares (OLS) estimate of* $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ *minimizes the SSR via a mathematical solution*
  - Can calculate the best $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ with matrix algebra. OLS has a simple "closed-form" formula:

$$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}$$

## Properties of the OLS estimator

- When the assumptions hold, OLS estimates are **BLUE**
  - **B**est: smallest possible sampling variance
  - For a **L**inear combination of the data
  - And **U**nbiased: on average the correct answer across samples
    - **B**est **L**inear **U**nbiased **E**stimator
- These properties are asymptotic, but OLS can also work well for small *N*
  - Easy to find $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ even in small samples
- Note a common mistake: referring to the **linear regression model** as an **OLS model.** OLS is not a model; it is an estimator
  - E.g., Linear regression models can also be estimated by maximum likelihood

![](images/blue-man-group.jpeg){width=50% fig-alt="The Blue Man Group drumming on paint-covered drums."}

### Variance of the error & R^2^: explained variation

- The residuals are used to estimate the variance of the error:

$$Var(\widehat{r}) = \frac{1}{N - K - 1}\sum_{i = 1}^{N}(y_{i} - {\widehat{y}}_{i})^{2} = s^{2}$$

- *R*^2^ is the percent of the variation in *y* explained by the independent variables

$$R^{2} = \frac{Var(\widehat{y})}{Var(\widehat{y}) + Var(\widehat{r})} = \frac{Explained\ Variation}{Total\ Variation}$$

- For example, if the *R*^2^ from a model regressing wages (DV) on gender (IV) is 0.05 this indicates that gender explains 5% of the variation in wages

## Assumptions of the model

1. Linearity
2. Not perfect collinearity
3. E(ε\|x) = 0
4. Homoscedastic errors
5. Uncorrelated errors
6. Normally distributed errors\*

![](images/linear-regression-errors.png){width=55% fig-alt="A straight regression line with normal error distributions of the same spread at several values of x."}

\*You will commonly hear people refer to an additional---but incorrect---assumption of the model: that variables (especially the DV) must be normally distributed. This does not have to be the case, and linear regression estimates tend to be quite robust even with highly non-normal data. See [Lumley et al. 2002](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.publhealth.23.100901.140546)

### Linearity

- *y* is linearly related to the *x*'s through the β's

$$y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2} + \varepsilon$$

- A unit change in *x~1~* has a constant effect on *y*
- However, just because the model is linear does not mean the effects have to be linear. E.g., If *x~1~* = sqrt(*w~1~*), then

$$y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1} + \beta_{2}x_{2} + \varepsilon = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\sqrt{w_{1}} + \beta_{2}x_{2} + \varepsilon$$

- A unit change in *x~1~* has a constant effect on *y*
- A unit change in *w~1~* does not have a constant effect on *y*

:::

### Homoscedastic errors

- Across all values of your IV ($\mathbf{x}$) you have the same variance for ε

$$Var(\varepsilon_{i}\,|\,\mathbf{x}_{i}) = \sigma^{2} \text{ for all } i \;\; (\sigma^{2} \text{ has no subscript } i)$$

- Can you think of when this would not be the case?
  - E.g., Where for some values of your IV your model predicts well (leading to a small variance of the errors at those values) but does not predict well at other values (leading to a large variance of the errors at those values)?

### Errors are uncorrelated

- Knowing the residual for one observation does not provide any systematic information about the residual of another observation
- Can you think of a situation where this would not be the case?
  - E.g., Where knowing how well the model predicts for one case, is associated with how well it predicts for other similar (or dissimilar) cases?

### Normally distributed errors

- The errors from your model should be approximately normally distributed for accurate significance testing
  - But, deviations from normality are common and usually do not cause major issues, especially with large datasets ([Lumley et al. 2002](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.publhealth.23.100901.140546))

### Collinearity

- We use multiple regression since the variables in $\mathbf{x}$ are correlated (collinear)
  - The variables in $\mathbf{x}$ cannot be **perfectly** collinear
    - Rarely the case unless by mistake (e.g., income in \$ *and* income in €)
  - Collinearity is rarely an issue for overall model inference or fit; can make interpretations of specific IVs problematic
    - If two IVs are explaining the same source of variation in the DV it can be difficult to isolate the effects of each
    - Can lead to puzzling situations such as when both IVs are non-significant in the model despite overall model fit increasing markedly when both variables are added to the model
      - Possible solutions:
        - Include only one or the other variable in the model
        - Combine the variables into one measure (e.g., [a scale or index](http://janda.org/workshop/scale%20construction/Talk/talk03.htm))

### Assessing multicollinearity

- The most common way to assess multicollinearity is to calculate variance inflation factors (VIFs)
  - Estimate a separate linear regression for each IV *x* where the IV is used as the dependent variable and all other IVs are used as predictors
  - Use the *R*^2^ from that model to calculate the VIF for that IV

$$VIF = \frac{1}{1 - R^{2}}$$

- No hard and fast rules for what VIF value is problematic
  - *"The VIF has a lower bound of 1 but no upper bound. Authorities differ on how high the VIF has to be to constitute a problem. Personally, I tend to get concerned when a VIF is greater than 2.50, which corresponds to an R^2^ of .60 with the other variables." ([Allison 2012](https://statisticalhorizons.com/multicollinearity))*
- Read more on when you can [safely ignore multicollinearity](https://statisticalhorizons.com/multicollinearity) and why dropping IVs just because they are collinear is [usually not a good idea](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1111/ssqu.12273)
- In Stata or R, easy to calculate VIFs

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_ah4", clear

reg income edyrs i.woman i.race age health subjclass role
estat vif
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
library(haven)           # import Stata data and labels
library(olsrr)           # variance inflation factors (VIFs)

ah4 <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_ah4.dta")

mod4 <- lm(income ~ edyrs + woman + as_factor(race) + age + health + subjclass + role,
  data = ah4)

ols_vif_tol(mod4)
```

:::
